concept.title: Cascade order and layers
concept.shortdesc: When declarations set the same property on the same element, CSS sorts them by precedence. It compares one criterion at a time. The first criterion that differs decides which declaration wins.

section.title: Sorting declarations
section.p: CSS Cascade 6 §2.1, Cascade Sorting Order; CSS Cascade 5 §6.1, Cascade Sorting Order; Selectors 4 §15, Calculating a selector’s specificity.
The cascade compares declarations in this order:
Each step matters only when the declarations tie at every preceding step.
CSS Cascade 5 §6.1, Cascade Sorting Order.

An origin identifies the source of a declaration. CSS defines user-agent, user, and author origins, plus animation and transition origins. Within the author, user, and user-agent origins, important declarations and normal declarations have different priorities. From highest to lowest, the CSS cascade order is:

ul.li: !important follows the value and raises that declaration above normal declarations in its origin. It does not make a declaration universally unbeatable. A higher-priority origin can still win.
CSSMedia’s stylesheet input consists of author stylesheets and built-in user-agent rules. It does not load a user-origin stylesheet.

section.p: CSS Cascade 6 §2.1, Cascade Sorting Order.

Some host environments divide a document into nested encapsulation contexts, such as shadow trees. For normal declarations, the outer context wins a tie against an inner context. For important declarations, the inner context wins. This comparison occurs after origin and importance, and before layers.
CSS Cascade 6 §2.1, Cascade Sorting Order; CSS Style Attributes §2, CSS Style Attributes.

When a host language defines a style attribute, declarations attached directly to an element take precedence over declarations from style rules at the same origin and importance. This rule is separate from selector specificity.
CSS Cascade 5 §6.4, Cascade Layers; CSS Cascade 5 §6.4.3, Layer Ordering.

@layer groups declarations within an origin. A layer’s order is established when its name first appears. A layer statement establishes order without adding rules. A layer block establishes a layer and contains its rules. Layers can be nested; a dotted name such as components.buttons identifies a sublayer.

For normal declarations, later layers outrank earlier layers. Unlayered declarations form an implicit final layer and outrank normal declarations in every named layer. For important declarations, this order is reversed: earlier layers outrank later layers, and layered important declarations outrank unlayered important declarations.
Within a parent layer, declarations assigned directly to the parent are ordered after its sublayers for normal declarations. Important declarations reverse that order as well.
All three declarations are normal and have the same specificity. The unlayered gray declaration wins. If all three declarations were important, the base layer would win.
Selectors 4 §15, Calculating a selector’s specificity.

Specificity compares the selector that matched. It is a three-part weight: ID selectors, class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, and type/pseudo-element selectors. Compare the parts from left to right. A larger earlier part takes precedence, regardless of the later parts.

For a selector list, the matching selector with the greatest specificity supplies the rule’s specificity. Specificity does not override origin, importance or layer order. See Specificity for how each selector form contributes.
CSS Cascade 6 §2.5, Scoping Styles: the @scope rule.

When declarations tie on origin, importance, layer and specificity, a declaration from a scope whose root is closer to the matched element wins. Count the ancestor steps from the element to each matching scope root. The smaller count is closer. An unscoped rule has no scope root and loses this tie-breaker to a scoped rule.
CSS Cascade 6 §2.1, Cascade Sorting Order.
If declarations still tie, the one that appears later wins. Imported rules take part at the position of their @import. Within one declaration block, the later declaration for the same property wins.

section.title: Scoped rules
section.p: CSS Cascade 6 §2.5, Scoping Styles: the @scope rule.

@scope limits the elements matched by its nested rules. The optional start selector identifies the scope root. The optional to selector identifies a scope limit: matching elements at the limit, and their descendants, are outside that scope.

This rule matches title elements inside a chapter scope, but not inside an appendix boundary. If the start selector is omitted, the document root is the scope root. A nested scope is relative to its enclosing scope.
Scope proximity affects precedence only after origin, importance, layer and specificity tie. It does not make a less-specific selector outrank a more-specific one.

section.title: Page-context declarations
section.p: CSS Paged Media 3 §4.4, Cascading in the page context; CSS GCPM 3 §3.1, Page Selectors; §3.2, Page groups.

Declarations in @page rules and page-margin rules cascade within their page context. Page selectors have their own specificity. A page type name contributes to the first component; :first and :blank contribute to the second; :left and :right contribute to the third. Each occurrence counts, including repeated pseudo-classes. The :nth() page pseudo-class contributes no specificity. It selects a page by its position in the document or, with a page-group name, its position in that group. When matching page rules tie on origin, importance, layer and specificity, source order decides. These declarations do not compete with declarations for an XML element.
